title: Buddhism: three refuges
hookLine: Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, the teaching and the community

lines: WHERE DO YOU GO WHEN IT RAINS?
cards: Where do you go when it rains hard? Not weather rain. The phone call with bad news, the month that goes sideways.
Shelters like that often go unnamed: a person to call first, a place, a book or a song. Buddhists name theirs, very precisely.
Three shelters, said aloud, often three times over, at the start of practice, at ceremonies, at the moment someone becomes a Buddhist. The third one is today's word: sangha.

teach.b: The three refuges, sometimes called the three jewels, are a short formula at the heart of Buddhist life. In Pali they begin: "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." I go to the Buddha for refuge.
Then the dhamma, the teaching. Then the sangha, the community. Then the whole thing is said a second time, and a third.
Saraṇa, refuge, means a shelter, a safe place, somewhere to stand. Buddhists explain it this way.

The Buddha is the example: proof, they say, that a human being can wake up. The dhamma is the map: the teaching and the path from this week, the four truths, impermanence, loving-kindness, the middle way.
And the sangha is the company for the road. Sangha means a gathering, a community, and Buddhists use it in more than one way.
In its traditional sense, it means the community of monks and nuns, who keep the teaching alive and are supported by lay Buddhists with food and care.
In another sense, it means the noble community: all those who've truly begun to wake up, in any age.

teach.h: NOT HALF: THE WHOLE OF IT.
teach.b: And some Buddhists today, especially in the West, use sangha for the whole community of practitioners, lay and monastic.
There's an exchange in the Samyutta Nikaya: the Buddha's attendant Ananda says good friendship is half of the holy life, and the Buddha corrects him. Not half, Ananda. The whole of it.
A path this long isn't meant to be walked alone.

how: Buddhists recite the three refuges, usually three times over, at the start of practice and at ceremonies; taking refuge formally is a common way of becoming Buddhist.

o: the community of the path, one of three refuges
a temple building where Buddhists go to meditate
a monk's vow to give up all his possessions

games.q: the three refuges — tap the pairs.
p: the example: a human can wake up

s: sangha has only one meaning for all Buddhists
the monastic community, the noble ones, or, for some today, all practitioners.
the refuges are usually said three times over
once, a second time, and a third.
the Buddha said good friendship is half the holy life
Ananda said half; the Buddha said it's the whole of it.

games.q: you're Ananda. you tell the Buddha that good friends are half of the spiritual life. what does he say?
o: no, Ananda: the whole of it.
games.why: in the Samyutta Nikaya the Buddha corrects Ananda: good friendship isn't half the holy life, it's the whole of it.

practice: Borrow the Buddhist shape, without the vow, and ask yourself three quiet questions: who shows me that a better way is possible, what words do I come back to when it's hard, and who walks with me?
Let a face, a line, a group come for each, and just notice them. Be grateful if gratitude comes.

wordCard.voice: Sangha. Pali for community: the third of Buddhism's three refuges, after the Buddha and the teaching. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: a gathering, a community.
